description: Vento Norte is a student experimental rocketry team at the Universidade do Estado do Amazonas (UEA/EST) in Manaus, Brazil. Our team works on the principle of learning through practice. By designing, building and launching experimental rockets, we give students the chance to apply classroom knowledge to a real engineering project from their first semesters, instead of waiting until the end of their degree.
summary:
IgaraPost is a collaborative environmental-monitoring Android mobile application focused on the Amazon, developed by team Vento Norte from the Universidade do Estado do Amazonas (UEA), the Amazonas state university. The platform integrates three sources of information. The first is geolocated community reports of smoke, fires and floods. The second is NASA satellite layers provided through GIBS, together with near-real-time fire detections from FIRMS. The third is an experimental NISAR radar explorer that allows two dates to be compared side by side. 
In response to the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge, the project places synthetic aperture radar at its core. In the Amazon, cloud cover and smoke frequently prevent observation by optical sensors, whereas radar can still observe the surface under these conditions. The application cross-checks each report against orbital data and highlights events not yet detected by satellites, so that community observation and remote sensing complement each other.
The proposal matters because riverside and peripheral communities are often the first affected by extreme events and the last to receive information. By working offline and using accessible language, IgaraPost turns NASA’s open data into alerts and records that are useful to these populations.
details:
IgaraPost is an environmental social network developed by the Vento Norte UEA team, from the Universidade do Estado do Amazonas (UEA), for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, in response to the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge. The project connects reports from local residents with Earth observation data to make environmental events in the Amazon easier to understand. It currently focuses on three categories: smoke, fires and floods.

The idea came from the need to bring scientific information closer to people’s everyday reality. Satellite imagery can show large stretches of territory, while residents can describe local impacts, such as smoke in a community, fire near homes or water reaching streets and crops. IgaraPost brings these perspectives together in an interface designed for residents of urban, rural and riverside areas, as well as students, educators and researchers.

In the app, users can record an observation with a description, category, date, location and photo. Reports can be browsed in a feed and on an interactive map, with comments, community following and filters. Organizing reports by territory and theme lets users follow nearby events and look up information about other places. Explanatory content helps the public interpret the data shown.

To put observations in context, the project integrates several information sources. Heat spot records use data from INPE’s Programa Queimadas and queries to NASA FIRMS. The map also gives access to layers from NASA’s Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS), including visualizations of aerosols, floods and surface water. Among them is the OPERA DSWx-S1 product, derived from Sentinel-1 radar. Each source adds a specific perspective, and its dates, coverage and limitations are respected.

The connection to the challenge comes mainly through the NISAR Explorer, which lets users compare radar images from different dates with a slider. The NISAR mission, a collaboration between NASA and ISRO, uses synthetic aperture radar to observe changes on the Earth’s surface, even through clouds and at night, which matters a lot in the Amazon. In the prototype, the explorer uses visualizations provided by GIBS and a local case study with preview NISAR products distributed by ASF DAAC. The comparisons are presented as experimental analyses; interpreting these changes environmentally requires processing calibrated data and further validation.

The app uses React, JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the interface, Vite to build the application, Leaflet for the maps and Capacitor to package it for Android. Local data is organized in JSON files, and on-device storage keeps reports, preferences and operations waiting to be sent. This lets the app keep local records when connectivity is limited, while queries to external sources need internet access. The solution was designed to run on smartphones and doesn’t require users to have any special sensing equipment.

The creative differentiator is the combination of community participation, satellite image exploration and science education. An observation recorded by a resident can be viewed in the same place where environmental data and comparisons of the territory over time appear. Users thus help build a collective record and find resources to understand what sensors can observe. The project values both the knowledge of people who live in the region and the information produced by scientific institutions.

During development, we took into account irregular connectivity, ease of use on small screens, map performance and the need for clear language. The interface is available in Portuguese, English and Spanish. We also made sure to identify sources, show when each piece of data is from, and distinguish community reports from demonstration examples and experimental analyses. A key concern is making clear that the absence of a satellite detection may be due to limits in coverage, overpass time or data availability.

The current result is an Android prototype with features for recording, browsing, interaction and geospatial exploration. Next steps include deploying the server so reports can be shared between devices, expanding NISAR scientific processing and testing with users. The intended impact is to broaden access to environmental information, encourage citizen science and give more visibility to the experiences of Amazonian communities, building a bridge between observations made on the ground and changes observed from space.

We used generative artificial intelligence tools, including ChatGPT and Claude, to help structure the proposal, analyze the app’s code, identify problems and draft text. Decisions about goals, priorities and scope were made by the team. The sources of the Earth observation data used in the project are identified, and the AI’s help with development does not mean the reports or environmental interpretations have been scientifically validated.
